questions.title: Is GSPO still an unbiased importance sampling estimator after applying length normalization?
questions.question_body: In Equation (4), GSPO defines the sequence-level importance ratio as s_i(\theta) = (\pi_\theta(y_i|x)/\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_i|x))^{1/|y_i|}. In standard importance sampling, I would expect the unnormalized ratio \pi_\theta(y_i|x)/\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_i|x). Raising it to the power 1/|y_i| seems to change the estimator. Without clipping, is the gradient in Equation (7) an unbiased estimator of the on-policy policy gradient under \pi_\theta, or is the length normalization a variance-reduction heuristic that introduces bias? If it is biased, what objective (if any) is GSPO optimizing exactly?

questions.title: Why is the token-level importance ratio in GRPO considered a misapplication of importance sampling?
questions.question_body: The paper argues GRPO misapplies importance sampling by using a token-level ratio w_{i,t}(\theta) = \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})/\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t}) based on a single sample at each position t. I understand that importance sampling typically requires averaging over many samples to reduce variance, but the estimator can still be unbiased with a single sample per state-action, right? Can you clarify precisely which expectation GRPO is (or is not) trying to estimate, and why applying the per-token ratio inside the sum over t breaks the intended distribution correction for the sequence-level reward? A small worked example contrasting token-level and sequence-level correction would help.

questions.title: What trust-region does GSPO’s sequence-level clipping actually enforce?
questions.question_body: PPO’s clipping is often interpreted as a proxy for a KL trust region at the action level. For GSPO, clipping is applied to the sequence-level ratio s_i(\theta) = exp\big((1/|y_i|)\sum_t \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}\big). Does clipping s_i(\theta) in [1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon] imply a bound on the average per-token KL or the length-normalized sequence KL, e.g., \frac{1}{|y|}\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(\cdot|x)\,\Vert\,\pi_\theta(\cdot|x))? If there is a formal connection, could you derive it? If not, how should we interpret the constraint that GSPO enforces geometrically on the policy update?

questions.title: How is KL regularization incorporated with GSPO in practice?
questions.question_body: The PPO objective usually includes a KL penalty to a reference policy. The paper omits the KL term for brevity. For GSPO, is the KL penalty applied at the sequence level (e.g., a penalty on \sum_t \mathrm{KL}_t or its length-normalized average), or at the token level as an auxiliary loss? Does the presence of a KL penalty interact with the sequence-level clipping range choices, and how should one set its coefficient relative to the GSPO clipping \varepsilon?

questions.title: Does equal token weighting in GSPO harm intra-sequence credit assignment?
questions.question_body: In Equation (7), GSPO ends up weighting all tokens in a response equally via the factor s_i(\theta) \widehat{A}_i, whereas GRPO gives each token its own importance ratio. Conceptually, if the reward r(x,y) is due to a few crucial tokens (e.g., a decisive reasoning step), won’t equal weighting dilute the gradient signal for those key tokens? Is the intent that GSPO-token (Equation (8)) should be used when finer credit assignment is necessary? If so, how would you recommend defining \widehat{A}_{i,t} to reflect partial credit (e.g., stepwise verifier signals) while keeping stability?

questions.title: Deriving GSPO’s gradient from an off-policy objective without heuristics
questions.question_body: Could you show a derivation that starts from a clear target objective (e.g., maximizing \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}, y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]) and applies exact importance sampling to use off-policy samples y\sim\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(\cdot|x), leading to the GSPO gradient in Equation (7)? In particular, where does the 1/|y| exponent on the ratio arise from in a principled way, rather than as a heuristic variance control?

questions.title: Practical handling of zero or tiny group standard deviation in \widehat{A}_i
questions.question_body: The group-based advantage is defined as a z-score: \widehat{A}_i = (r(x,y_i)-\mathrm{mean})/\mathrm{std}. What happens when all G responses get identical rewards (\mathrm{std} = 0) or when \mathrm{std} is extremely small, which can happen with sparse or binary verifiers? Do you add an \epsilon to the denominator, cap \widehat{A}_i, or fall back to mean-centering without scaling? Any stability tips here would be appreciated.

questions.title: How should s_i(\theta) be computed across multiple mini-batch updates from one rollout batch?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions partitioning a large rollout batch into several mini-batches, which makes subsequent updates progressively more off-policy. During these mini-batch updates, do you compute s_i(\theta) against the same fixed \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} that generated the rollouts, or do you refresh \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} between mini-batches? From an importance sampling standpoint, only the behavior policy that actually generated the samples should appear in the denominator, so I am unsure whether re-evaluating with a changing \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} would introduce bias or instability.

questions.title: Choosing and interpreting GSPO clipping ranges of 3e-4 and 4e-4
questions.question_body: In the experiments, the left and right clipping ranges for GSPO are set to 3e-4 and 4e-4, which are very small compared to GRPO’s 0.2 and 0.27. How should practitioners select these ranges for a new model/task? Are these numbers tied to typical distributions of s_i(\theta) across batches after the 1/|y| normalization? Is there a rule of thumb relating the target average per-token KL to a corresponding range for s_i(\theta)?

questions.title: Why is sequence likelihood more stable than token likelihood under MoE routing volatility?
questions.question_body: Section 5.3 argues that although MoE expert activation can change substantially token-to-token after updates, the sequence likelihood \pi_\theta(y|x) does not fluctuate drastically, making s_i(\theta) stable. Can you provide intuition or empirical evidence for this claim? For instance, is there a bound showing that the cumulative effect of routing changes largely cancels out in the log-likelihood sum, or that shared experts dominate the likelihood for most tokens?

questions.title: Numerical robustness of using inference-engine likelihoods at the sequence level
questions.question_body: You note that GSPO can use likelihoods returned by an inference engine (e.g., vLLM) instead of recomputing them in the training engine, due to higher tolerance at the sequence level. Since s_i(\theta) uses exp of an average of log ratios, it still aggregates per-token log-probs. How large can floating-point precision or kernel differences be before this becomes problematic? Have you observed measurable training drift when mixing engines, and do you recommend any calibration or consistency checks before adopting this optimization?

questions.title: Equivalence of GSPO to on-policy REINFORCE with a group baseline when \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} = \pi_\theta
questions.question_body: If we consider a purely on-policy setting where \pi_{\theta_\text{old}} = \pi_\theta and turn off clipping, then s_i(\theta) = 1 and Equation (7) becomes \mathbb{E}[\widehat{A}_i \cdot \frac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})]. Is this exactly REINFORCE with a per-group z-scored baseline? If there are any subtle differences (e.g., length normalization), could you point them out and explain their impact?

questions.title: Does sequence-level clipping risk discarding informative early-token gradients?
questions.question_body: With GSPO, if s_i(\theta) is clipped (or if the min operator picks the clipped branch), the entire sequence’s contribution is modulated uniformly. Could this overly suppress learning signals for early tokens that are reliably good, just because later tokens made the sample too off-policy? Have you tried hybrid schemes that clip at the sequence level but allow limited per-token adjustments for tokens whose local ratios are close to 1?

questions.title: Can you provide a formal variance comparison between GSPO and GRPO as sequence length grows?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that GRPO’s token-level ratios induce high-variance gradient estimates that accumulate with length, while GSPO’s sequence-level approach reduces variance. Is there a formal variance analysis (even under simplifying assumptions, e.g., independent tokens) that shows how the variance of the gradient estimator scales with |y| for the two methods? A comparison of asymptotic behavior with respect to |y| and G would clarify the source of GSPO’s stability.

questions.title: Why define s_{i,t}(\theta) with a stop-gradient ratio in GSPO-token?
questions.question_body: In Equation (9), s_{i,t}(\theta) = \mathrm{sg}[s_i(\theta)] \cdot \frac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\mathrm{sg}[\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})]}. Since this product is numerically equal to s_i(\theta), why not simply use s_i(\theta) directly at each token and rely on autodiff? Is the purpose to ensure that the gradient only flows through \log \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}|\cdot) and not through s_i(\theta), thereby matching Equation (11)? A brief explanation of the autodiff implications would help.

questions.title: How does group size G affect stability when using z-scored advantages?
questions.question_body: GSPO and GRPO both use a group-based advantage computed by z-scoring rewards over G sampled responses for the same x. What happens when G is small (e.g., G = 2 or 3), or even G = 1 (undefined)? Is there a recommended minimum G for stability, and how sensitive are the gradients to the stochasticity of the sample mean and standard deviation estimates as G varies?

questions.title: Handling tasks with partial credit or multi-turn rewards under GSPO
questions.question_body: The paper notes GSPO-token can allow token-wise advantage customization for scenarios like multi-turn RL. Suppose we have partial credit signals at intermediate turns or steps. Would you recommend computing a separate \widehat{A}_{i,t} per step using a per-step verifier and then aggregating with GSPO-token, or computing several sequence-level \widehat{A}_i for segments and summing their contributions? Any guidance on preventing leakage of future rewards when defining per-token advantages in a causal manner?

questions.title: Interpreting the paradox of higher clipping fractions yet better efficiency under GSPO
questions.question_body: Figure 2 suggests GSPO clips a much larger fraction of tokens (or sequences) than GRPO but still trains more efficiently. Could you formalize why a higher raw clipping fraction does not necessarily imply lower effective sample size? For example, is the relevant metric the variance of the retained gradient estimator rather than the count of unclipped tokens, and does GSPO’s uniform per-sequence weighting reduce estimator variance enough to outweigh the apparent loss due to more clipping?

questions.title: What objective is optimized if we remove clipping from GSPO and set \widehat{A}_i to raw rewards?
questions.question_body: If we consider GSPO without clipping and define \widehat{A}_i = r(x,y_i) - b(x) with some baseline b(x) (not z-scored, to avoid dependence on G), what exact objective is being optimized when using off-policy samples y_i\sim\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}? Is there a clean expression showing that the estimator converges to the gradient of \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}[r(x,y)] (or a length-normalized variant) under certain conditions, or is the 1/|y| exponent essential enough that we should view this as optimizing a surrogate different from expected reward?
